readerTitle: Same coffee machine, two very different sales
caseNote: 가상 사례 (커피 머신 구매 장면, 사무용 의자 매장, 사내 교육팀) · 실제 기업·수치 없음
insight: 기업 고객과 개인 고객의 진짜 차이는 주문 규모가 아니라, 구매자가 그 결정을 다른 사람 앞에서 변호해야 하느냐다. 기업 고객에게는 제품과 함께 '설득할 근거'를 팔아야 한다.
misconception: 기업 고객은 큰 개인 고객일 뿐이라 같은 매력 포인트를 더 크게, 더 싸게 제시하면 된다.

sources.text: 마케팅의 표준 개념 (B2B와 B2C 구매 의사결정의 차이)
모든 장면과 인물은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 인물은 가상이며 통계나 실제 기업 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. '5주, 견적 3개' 등은 설명용 표현입니다.
CUS-09-01(구매자 vs 사용자), CUS-09-02(구매 위원회), CUS-09-03(기업 구매의 위험), MKT-08-05(영업 주도 vs 셀프서브)와 내용이 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요. 이 레슨은 '결정을 변호해야 하는가'라는 관점에만 집중하고 채널 선택은 다음 레슨으로 넘겼습니다.

cards.title: Same coffee machine, two very different sales
body: On Saturday, Maya buys an espresso machine for her kitchen. She reads a few reviews, likes how it looks, and pays within twenty minutes.
On Monday, she's asked to buy the same machine for her office. It takes five weeks, three quotes, a service contract and her boss's sign-off.
Same person. Same machine. The product didn't change. The decision did.

image.label: One woman buying the same espresso machine at home and at the office
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 주말 매장에서 커피 머신을 들고 웃으며 바로 계산하는 여성, 오른쪽은 같은 여성이 사무실에서 같은 머신 사진 옆에 견적서 3장, 계약서, 결재 도장이 쌓인 책상 앞에 앉아 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A company wants 40 of your chairs.
body: You run a shop selling ergonomic office chairs. Shoppers come in, sit down, and usually buy on the spot. Your showroom is your best sales tool.
An office manager emails: her company needs 40 chairs for a new floor. What do you send back?

options.text: A warm invite to the showroom so she can try every model
options.feedback: Trying the chair is how you win shoppers, and it builds trust. But it doesn't give her anything to show the people who must approve the purchase.

options.text: A one-page summary: price per chair, warranty, delivery dates, return terms
options.feedback: Less exciting than a showroom visit, but it answers the questions she'll face from finance. You're making her job easy, not just selling a chair.

options.text: A 15% bulk discount, offered right away
options.feedback: A lower price helps, but you give away margin before you know what she needs. Price is rarely her only worry.

cards.title: Liking the chair wasn't her problem.
body: She had already sat in one of your chairs. She liked it.
Her real problem was Thursday's meeting, where finance would ask: Why these? Why this price? What if they break? Can we return them? She needed answers she could repeat when you weren't in the room.
A tidy one-page summary does that work for her. A friendly showroom invite leaves her to do it alone.

image.label: Office manager forwarding a one-page summary to her boss
image.brief: 사무실 책상에서 여성 관리자가 한 장짜리 요약서를 상사에게 전달하는 장면. 요약서에는 "Price", "Warranty", "Delivery", "Returns" 네 줄만 보임. 뒤쪽 회의실에 재무팀 사람들이 기다리는 모습. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Selling to businesses vs consumers
body: When you sell to consumers, people usually spend their own money on something for themselves. If it disappoints, they're the only one who pays.
When you sell to businesses, someone spends the company's money, often for other people, and must explain the choice later. A bad pick can cost them credibility at work.
So the real gap isn't the size of the order. It's that the **business buyer has to defend the decision**.
cards.softwareNote: The same app can sell both ways. A person tries it free and pays by card. A company asks about security, admin controls, invoices and contracts, because someone must sign off on it.

cards.title: One difference changes the whole sale.
body: Because the business buyer must justify the choice, almost everything about the sale shifts.
list: **Who decides:** often one person vs several people who must agree
**Whose money:** their own vs a budget someone else watches
**What's at risk:** a disappointing purchase vs their reputation at work
**How long it takes:** minutes or days vs weeks or months
**What wins:** feel, price and ease vs proof, clear terms and support
cards.callout: Consumers ask, "Do I want this?" Business buyers also ask, "Can I justify this?"
cards.softwareNote: In software, this is why business plans list uptime, support hours and data policies, things an individual user rarely reads.

cards.title: Watch who must justify, not the name on the invoice.
body: A café owner buying a coffee grinder is technically a business. But she spends her own money and answers to nobody, so she often buys like a consumer.
A family choosing a car can act like a company: several people, a set budget, long debates, and one person who must explain the choice to the others.
The useful question is simple: who has to justify this purchase, and to whom?

image.label: A café owner buying alone next to a family debating a car
image.brief: 두 장면 나란히. 왼쪽은 카페 사장이 혼자 그라인더를 고르고 바로 결제하는 모습, 오른쪽은 가족 네 명이 자동차 앞에서 예산표를 들고 토론하는 모습. 각 장면 위에 "Who must I convince?" 말풍선. 실제 차량 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Business buyers are still people.
body: B2B buyers feel excitement, trust and fear just like shoppers. A dry spec sheet with no reason to care rarely wins on its own.
And don't bury small buyers in paperwork. A ten-page proposal for a two-person firm adds work, not confidence.
Match your effort to how much justifying the buyer really has to do. Too little, and they can't defend you. Too much, and you slow down a yes.

cards.title: Now you're the training team.
body: You run training inside a large company. Your one-day course on handling difficult customers gets great reviews from employees who sign up on their own.
Now you want a department head to send her whole team of 20. What leads your pitch?

options.text: Glowing quotes from employees who loved the course
options.feedback: It shows the course is well run. But she's giving up 20 days of her team's work, and enjoyment isn't what her boss will ask about.

options.text: What the team will do differently afterward, the cost in hours, and a small pilot first
options.feedback: You trade a fast yes for one she can defend. The pilot also lowers her personal risk if the course disappoints.

options.text: A free seat for her, so she can see how good it is
options.feedback: A kind gesture that treats her like a consumer. She may love it and still have nothing to show the people she answers to.

cards.title: Ask who has to defend the purchase.
body: Consumers buy what they want. Business buyers buy what they can justify. Give each the thing they need to say yes.
**Try it today:** pick one business customer. Write the three questions their boss or finance team will ask, and make sure your offer answers each one in a single line.
